Now if we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or precious stone, shaped by the craft and design of men.
For God overlooked those times of ignorance, and now he commands all people, at every time and in every place, to repent;
for he has fixed a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has appointed, and he has given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead."
But when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, and others said: "We will hear you about this again."
And so Paul went out from among them.
But some followed him and believed. Among them were Dionysius the Areopagite and his wife, named Damaris, and others with them.
After this Paul left the Athenians and came to Corinth.
And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had just come from Italy, and Priscilla his wife (for Claudius Caesar had ordered all the Jews to be expelled from Rome); he went to them,
and because they knew the same craft, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers [?] by trade.
And every Sabbath he spoke in the synagogue and tried to persuade Jews and Gentiles.
And when Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul was pressed by the Spirit, and he testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
But when they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his garment at them and said to them: "Your blood be upon your own heads! May I be innocent! From now on I will go to the Gentiles."
And he left there and went into the house of a certain man named Titius, son of Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house [?] adjoined the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his household. Many Corinthians listened to him, and they believed and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul at night in a vision: "Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will lay hands on you to harm you, for I have many people in this city."
And he stayed there one year and six months and taught the word of God among them.
Now when Gallio was governor of Achaia, all the Jews rose up together against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
and they said: "This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law."
And when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews: "If it were some offence or wicked deed, O Jews, I would have borne with you, as your complaint requires;
but if it is some dispute about words and names and your law, see to it yourselves, for I do not wish to be a judge of such matters."
And he drove them away from the judgment seat.
Then all the Gentiles seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judgment seat; and Gallio paid no attention to any of this.
But Paul stayed there many days, and then took leave of the brothers and sailed by ship to Syria, and with him were Priscilla and Aquila. He had his hair cut at Cenchreae, for he had made a vow.
He arrived at Ephesus and left them there, and he himself went into the synagogue and spoke with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay there, he did not consent,
but took leave of them and said: "I will come back again, if God wills." He boarded a ship from Ephesus
and went down to Caesarea; he went up and greeted the church, and then went to Antioch.
And after spending some time there he left, and went from place to place, one after another, through the regions of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
There was a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man, who came to Ephesus; he was powerful in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Aquila and Priscilla heard him, and they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
And when he wanted to cross over to Achaia, they wrote to the brothers, the disciples, to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace,
for he powerfully refuted the Jews in front of the people, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul passed through the upper regions and came to Ephesus, and there he found some disciples
and said to them: "Have you received the Holy Spirit since you believed?" And they said to him: "No, we have not even heard of the Holy Spirit."
Paul said to them, "Into what, then, were you baptized?" And they said, "Into John's baptism."
Paul said to them, "John baptized the people with the baptism of repentance, and he told them to believe in the one who was coming after him, that is, Jesus Christ."
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ,
and when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
There were twelve of these men in all.
And he went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months, speaking and persuading them about the kingdom of God.

When some of them became angry and disobedient and spoke evil of the Way in front of the crowd, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, and every day he spoke in the school of Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, until all who lived in Asia, both Jews and gentiles, had heard the word of the Lord.
God worked no small power through Paul's hands,
so that even kerchiefs and cloths that had touched his sweat were carried to the sick, and the diseases left them and the unclean spirits went out.
Some of the wandering Jewish exorcists began to name the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, "We adjure you by Jesus, whom Paul preaches."
There were seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish high priest, who were doing this.
The evil spirit answered them, "Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?"
And the man who had the unclean spirit rose up, overpowered both of them and attacked them, until they fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and gentiles living in Ephesus. Fear fell upon all of them, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many of those who believed came and confessed their deeds.
Many who had practised evil arts gathered their books and burned them in front of everyone. They counted up their value and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.
In this way the word of the Lord grew mightily and multiplied.
When these things were completed, Paul resolved in his heart to go to Jerusalem after passing through Macedonia and Achaia, and he said, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome."
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed in Asia for a time.
At that time there was no small fear because of the Way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, made silver shrines of Artemis and brought no small amount of business to the craftsmen.
He gathered them together with the workers in related trades and said, "Men, you know that our livelihood comes from this business.
You see and hear that Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

This is not only a hardship for us, that this place [i.e. our trade?] is in danger of being discredited for us. The temple of the great goddess Artemis is also in danger of being despised, and her wealth of being destroyed, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
When they heard this, they were filled with anger, and they cried out, saying: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
And the whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed together into the theatre, and they seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Paul's company, from the gathering.
But Paul wanted to go in among the people, and the disciples did not let him.
And some of the officials of Asia, who were his friends, sent to him and urged him not to give himself up to the theatre.
Some were shouting one thing and some another, for the crowd was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had gathered.
And they brought Alexander forward out of the crowd, for the Jews had put him forward. And Alexander motioned with his hand to the people and wanted to make a defence before the people.
When they realized that he was a Jew, all of them with one voice kept crying out together for as long as two hours, saying: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

The town clerk of the people motioned with his hand and said: "Men of the people, Ephesians, who is there among men who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the temple-keeper of the great Artemis and of the Diopetes?
Since this is undeniable, you ought to be calm and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of shrines nor blasphemers of our god.
If Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, let them bring the market-men of the quarters [?], and there are governors; let them bring charges against one another.
But if anything further is to be inquired into, let it be settled in a lawful assembly.
For we are in danger of being accused over today's riot, since there was no cause for which we could give an account of this gathering." And when he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the riot had died down, Paul called the disciples and encouraged them, and he took his leave and set out to go to Macedonia.
And he went through those regions and encouraged them with many words, and from there he went to Greece.
And he was there three months. There too a plot was made against him by the Jews, as he was about to go up to Syria, so he decided to return there by way of Macedonia.
And with him as far as Asia went Sosipater son of Pyrrhus, of Beroea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and of the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus.
These went on ahead of us and waited for us at Troas.
We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and came to them at Troas on the fifth day, and we stayed there seven days.

And on the first day of the week we were gathered together for the blessing of bread. And Paul was speaking to them the word of teaching, for he was to depart the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.

A certain young man named Eutychus was sitting at the window. And as he was overcome by deep sleep while Paul spoke for a long time, he fell down asleep, fell from the third storey to the ground, and lay dead.
Paul went down and fell upon him, embraced him, and said: "Do not be troubled, for his life is still in him."
And he went up from there, blessed the bread and ate, and conversed for a long time until dawn, and then departed.
They brought the boy alive, and they were comforted not a little.
But we went ahead by ship and went up to Assos [?: the text reads "Nason"], intending to take Paul on board there, for he had arranged it so, since he meant to come on foot.
When he came to us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene.
From there we sailed the next day and arrived off Chios. In the evening we came to Samos, and the following day to Miletus.
Paul wanted to sail past Ephesus, so that he would not spend a long time in Asia, for he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, if that were possible for him.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the church.
When they came to him, he said to them: "You yourselves know how I was with you the whole time, from the first day I came into Asia,
serving the Lord with all humility and tears, and in the trials that befell me through the plots of the Jews;
how I held back nothing that was good for you, but told it to you and taught you before the people and in your houses,
testifying to Jews and Gentiles about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, behold, bound in the spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, and I do not know what will happen to me there,
except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in city after city and tells me that bonds and afflictions await me.

But I have not counted myself more precious than my soul, so that I may finish my course and my ministry, which I received from the Lord Jesus Christ: the testimony and the gospel of the grace of God.
And now, behold, I know that none of you will see my face again, all of you among whom I went about preaching the kingdom.
And so I testify to you on this very day that I am innocent of the blood of all of you,
for I held nothing back, but declared to you the whole counsel [lit. care] of God.
So keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you overseers and shepherds of the churches of God, which he obtained with his own blood.
I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, who will not spare the flock.
And men will rise up from among you who will speak perverse things, to draw the disciples away after them.
So be watchful, and remember that for three years, night and day, I did not stop teaching each one of you.
And now, brothers, I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among all the saints.
My heart did not desire anyone's silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands of mine provided for my needs and for those who were with me.
And I showed you in everything that by working hard like this we must help the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for he said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"
When he had said this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.
Everyone wept loudly, and they threw their arms around Paul's neck and kissed him.
with weeping, most of all at the word he had spoken, that they would no longer see his face. And they were sending him off to the ship.
And when we had gone aboard the ship, we parted from them. We sailed quickly and reached Cos, the next day Rhodes, and from there Patara.
And we found a ship that was crossing over to Phoenicia. We went aboard and set sail on it.
When Cyprus came into view, we left it on our left and sailed on toward Syria, and we reached Tyre, for there the ship's cargo was to be unloaded.
And we sought out the brothers and stayed only seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
And when the seven days were over, we left and were on our way. They escorted us, with their households and children, as far as outside the city, and they knelt down on the seashore and prayed.
We said farewell to one another and boarded the ship, and they returned to their own place.
And we came by ship from Tyre and reached Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day.
The next day we left there and came to Caesarea. We went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four daughters who were prophetesses.
And we stayed there many days. A prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said: "Thus says the Holy Spirit: 'The man to whom this belt belongs, the Jews will bind like this in Jerusalem and hand him over into the hands of the Gentiles.'"
When we heard this, we and the people of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

Then Paul answered and said to us: "What are you doing, weeping and grieving my heart? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem; I am prepared for the sake of the name of the Lord Jesus."
And since we could not persuade him, we fell silent and said: "May the will of God be done."
After those days we made ready and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us, and we brought along the man with whom we were to stay, Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple.
When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went with us to James, and all the elders came.
He greeted them and told them one by one what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard this, they glorified God and said to him: "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews? They are all zealous for the Law.
Some say about you that you teach the Jews who live among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, and some say about you that they should not circumcise their children or walk according to the customs.
What, then, is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
Do what I tell you: there are men among us who are under a vow of their own.
Take these men and purify yourself with them, so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what they say about you is nothing, but that you yourself also live by and keep the Law.

"But concerning the Gentiles who have believed, we have written and commanded that they need observe nothing of this kind, except that they keep themselves from what is sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from fornication."
Then the next day Paul took those men, purified himself with them, and went into the temple to announce the completion of the days of purification, until the offering was made for each one of them.
When the seven days were nearly completed, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple. They stirred up all the people, laid their hands on him, and

cried out: "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who plots evil against the people, the law and this place, and teaches the same to everyone everywhere. Besides that, he has brought Gentiles into the temple and has defiled this holy place."
For they had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, and there was a great uproar among the people. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, word reached the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem had gathered together.
He immediately took soldiers and centurions and came down on them. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the commander came up, brought him out, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing and some another. Since he could not find out anything because of the uproar, he ordered Paul to be taken into the barracks.
When he reached the steps, Paul had to be carried up by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the mass of people followed, crying out and saying, "Away with him!"
As he was being brought into the barracks, Paul said to the commander, "May I say something to you?" He replied, "Do you know Greek?
Then are you not the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?"
Paul said to him, "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, let me speak to the people."
When he had given him permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the people with his hand. When there was silence, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying:
"Brothers and fathers, listen to the defence I now make to you."
When they heard that he was speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said:

"I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city and educated at the feet of Gamaliel. I was strictly taught the law of our fathers, and I was zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prison,

as the high priest and all the elders can testify about me. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I was going to Damascus to bring those who were there to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.
As I was on my way and drawing near to Damascus, about noon, a great light from heaven suddenly shone upon me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice that said to me: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
I answered: "Who are you, Lord?" He said to me: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."
Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the words spoken to me.
I said: "And what shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me: "Get up and go to Damascus, and there you will be told what you have been commanded to do."
And since I could not see because of the glory of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and I went into Damascus.
There was a man named Ananias, a God-fearing man according to the law, who was well spoken of by all the Jews living in Damascus.
He came to me, stood over me and said to me: "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very moment I received my sight and looked at him.
And he said: "The God of our fathers has chosen you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth,
for you will be his witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, do not delay. Get up, be baptized, wash away your sins and call on his name."
And it happened that when I returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw the Lord, and he said to me: "Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me."
And I said: "Lord, they themselves know that I was the one who handed over to prison and tortured in the synagogues those who believed in you.
And when the blood of Stephen, your witness, was being shed, I too was standing by and guarding the garments of those who killed him."
And he said to me: "Go, for I will send you far away to the nations."
They listened to him up to this word. Then they raised their voices and said: "Take such a man off the earth, for he is not fit to live."
And as they were shouting, they were throwing off their garments and flinging dust up into the air.
The tribune ordered that he be brought into the barracks, and said: "I will examine him under torture, so that I may learn for what crime they are shouting against him like this."
And as they were stretching him out with straps, Paul said to the centurion who stood there: "Is it lawful for you to torture a Roman man who has not been tried?"
When the centurion heard this, he told the tribune, saying: "What are you about to do? This man is a Roman."
The tribune came to Paul and said to him: "Tell me, are you a Roman?" And he said: "Yes."
The tribune answered and said: "I acquired this status for a great sum of money." And Paul said: "But I was born in it."
Then those who were about to torture him immediately drew back from him. And the tribune was afraid when he realized that Paul was a Roman and that he had been entrusted to him.

On the next day, wanting to find out more exactly why the Jews were accusing him like this, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. They brought Paul and stood him among them.
Paul looked at the council and said: "Men, brothers, I have lived before God with an entirely good conscience to this very day."
Then the high priest Ananias ordered those standing before him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit as a judge according to the law, and against the law you order me to be struck?"
But those standing before him said to him: "Do you revile the high priest of God?"
Paul said: "I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest, for it is written: 'You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people.'"

When Paul realized that one part of the council was of the Sadducees and the other part of the Pharisees, he cried out in the council: "Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee and the son of a Pharisee; it is for the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged."
When he said this, there was a great uproar between the Sadducees and the Pharisees, and the multitude of the people was [?] divided.
For the Sadducees say: "There is no resurrection of the dead, nor angel, nor spirit," but the Pharisees acknowledge all of these.
And there was a great outcry. And some of the scribes of the party of the Pharisees stood up and contended, saying: "We find nothing evil in this man. A spirit has spoken to him, or else an angel."
And as the uproar grew great, the tribune was afraid that Paul would be torn apart by them. He ordered the soldiers to go down and snatch him out from among them and bring him into the barracks.
On the following night the Lord stood over him and said: "Do not be afraid, for just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome."
And when day broke, the Jews held a gathering and bound themselves under a curse, and said that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty who made this conspiracy.
They went to the high priests and the elders and said: "We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
Now you, together with the council, inform the tribune so that he brings him down to you, as though you wished to learn more accurately about him; and we are ready to kill him before he comes near."
Paul's nephew heard this talk. He went and entered the barracks and told it to Paul.
Then Paul called one of the centurions and said: "Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him."
So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said: "The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you."
The tribune took him by the hand, led him aside, and asked: "What is it that you have to tell me?"
He said: "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to their council tomorrow, as though to examine him more accurately.

But do not give in to them, for more than forty of their men are lying in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him. And now they are ready and are waiting for your order."
So the tribune dismissed the young man and ordered him to tell no one: "that you have informed me of this."
And he called two of the centurions and said: "Get ready two hundred of the soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, and seventy horsemen and two hundred shield-bearers, from the third hour of the night.
"And prepare an escort, so that they may mount Paul and bring him to Felix the governor."
And he wrote a letter, in which the following was written:
"The praised [?] Lysias to the most excellent Felix the governor: I greet you with joy.
This man had been seized by the Jews, and they were about to kill him. I came upon them with troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.
And because I wanted to understand the charge they were bringing against him, I brought him down to their council,
and I found that they were accusing him over questions of their law, and no charge worthy of death or of bonds was found against him.
And when I was informed of an evil plot against this man, I sent him to you, and I have ordered his accusers to speak before you. Farewell!"
Then the soldiers, as they had been commanded, took Paul and brought him by night as far as Antipatris.
And on the next day they let the horsemen go on, and returned to the camp.
And these entered Caesarea, gave the letter to the governor, and also presented Paul to him.
He read it and asked him, "What country are you from?" And he learned that he was a Cilician.
He said, "I will hear you when your accusers also come." And he ordered him to be kept in Herod's palace.
After five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and with an orator, a certain Tertullus, and they informed the governor against Paul.
And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: "Through you we enjoy much peace, and the good order that is being brought about in this nation by your counsel
we welcome always [?] and in all places, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.
So as not to weary you further, I beg you to hear us briefly in your kindness.
For we have found this man to be a pestilent fellow, one who stirred up disturbances among all the Jews throughout the world, a ringleader of the heresy of the Galileans,
who even tried to defile the temple, and whom we seized,
and by examining him yourself you will be able to learn about all these things of which we accuse him."
The other Jews also testified against him and said that it was so.
When the governor nodded to him, Paul answered and said: "Knowing that you have been judge of this nation for many years, I gladly make my defence.
You are able to verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
And they did not find me in the temple speaking with anyone or gathering a crowd of people, nor in the synagogues, nor in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.
But this I confess to you: that in the Way, which they call a heresy, I serve the God of the fathers, and I believe everything that is written in the prophets.
And I have hope toward God, which they themselves also await: that there is to be a resurrection of the righteous and of sinners.
For this reason I also strive, and I always have an unhindered mind toward God and toward people.
And after many years I came to bring alms for my nation, and offerings,
and in the course of these they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd or with any disturbance.
But there were certain Jews from Asia. They are the ones who ought to have come before you and made their accusation, if they have anything to say against me.
Or else let these men themselves say what fault they found in me when I stood in the council,
unless it is for that one statement that I cried out while I stood among them: 'It is for the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged by you.'"
Felix knew the facts about the Way accurately, and he put them off, saying: "When Lysias the tribune comes, then I will look into your case."
And he ordered the centurion to keep him in custody but to let him be at ease, and not to stop any of his own people from serving him.
After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jew. He summoned Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
And as Paul spoke about righteousness, self-restraint, and the judgment to come, Felix became afraid and said: "That is enough for now. Go, and when I have a free moment I will call for you."
At the same time he was hoping that Paul would give him money. For this reason he sent for him often and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Porcius Festus came to succeed Felix. Felix wanted to do the Jews a favour, so he left Paul in chains.
When Festus arrived in the province, after three days he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The high priests and the leaders of the Jews informed him about Paul.
They pleaded with him and asked him for a favour against Paul: that he would summon him to Jerusalem. Meanwhile they would lie in wait on the road to kill him.
But Festus told them that Paul was being kept at Caesarea, and that he himself would soon be leaving Jerusalem.
And he said: "Let those of you who are able come with me, and if there is anything wrong with that man, bring your accusation against him."
He stayed there no more than eight or ten days, and then went down to Caesarea. He sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When Paul came, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him and brought many serious charges against him, which they could not prove.
But Paul answered in his defence: "I have done nothing wrong, either against the law of the Jews or against Caesar."
But Festus wanted to do the Jews a favour, so he answered Paul: "Do you want to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there on these charges before me?"
Paul said to him: "I am standing at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you know very well.

If I have done wrong and have done something that deserves death, I do not try to escape death. But if I have done none of the things these men accuse me of, no one has the power to hand me over to them as a favour. I appeal to Caesar."
Then Festus conferred with his council and said: "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go."
And when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to greet Festus.
And as they stayed there many days, Festus told the king about Paul and said to him: "There is a certain man left behind by Felix as a prisoner,
about whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, and they asked for a sentence against him.

I answered them and said: 'It is not the custom of the Romans to hand over any man until the one who is accused has his accusers face to face and has an opportunity to make his defense against the charge.'
And when they had gathered here, I made no delay at all. On the next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought,
and his accusers stood up against him, but they brought forward no charge of the evil I had supposed.
They had certain disputes with him about their own demon, and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul says is alive.
And since I found nothing in investigating this, I asked him whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there about it.
But Paul cried out to be kept in custody, so that Caesar might take cognizance of the case. And I ordered him to be kept until I send him to Caesar."
Agrippa answered and said to Festus: "I too would like to hear the man." And he said to him: "Tomorrow you shall hear him."

On the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp [?]. And when they had entered the hall of judgment together with the commanders of a thousand and the men who were the leaders of the city, Festus gave the order and Paul came in.

And Festus said: "King Agrippa, and all you men who are here with us, do you see this man? About him the whole multitude of the Jews came to me in Jerusalem, and here too they cry out and say that he ought not to live any longer.
But I understood that he has done nothing worthy of death; and since he himself appealed to Caesar, I decided to send him.

I have nothing certain to write to my lord about him. For this reason I have brought him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that you may examine him and know what I should write to him.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner and not make known the charge against him."
And Agrippa said to Paul: "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul stretched out his hand and answered, saying:
"Concerning everything of which the Jews accuse me, King Agrippa, I count myself blessed, because today I am to make my defense before you above all.
For you are well acquainted with all the customs and disputes of the Jews, and you know them. Therefore I beg you, hear me patiently.
For all the Jews know my way of life from my youth, which was from the beginning among my own nation in Jerusalem.
They have known me from the beginning, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee, in accordance with the truth of our worship.
And now I stand and am judged because of the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving day and night, hope to attain. It is for this hope that I am accused, O king.
Why is it judged unbelievable among you that God raises the dead?
I myself thought that I ought to do many evil things against the name of Jesus the Nazarene,
which I also did in Jerusalem, for I shut up many saints in prison, for I had received authority from the chief priests to put them to death, and I took the count [?].
And in all the synagogues I tortured them many times and forced them to blaspheme, and raging all the more against them, I persecuted them even as far as the surrounding cities.
While doing this I was going to Damascus with the authority and command of the chief priests.
At midday on the road I saw, O king, a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those travelling with me.
And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice that said to me in the Hebrew language: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad."
I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and a witness of what you have seen of me and of what I will show you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you,

to open their eyes and to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of the devil to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of their sins and a share among those who are sanctified by faith in me."
Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to that heavenly vision,

but first to those in Damascus, and in Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I proclaimed repentance and turning to the living God, so that they should do works worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and plotted to kill me.
By the [?] that comes from God I stand to this very day and testify to small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets said would come to pass, and Moses:
that the Christ was to suffer, and that, as the first of the resurrection of the dead, he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles."
As he was saying this, Festus said in a loud voice: "You are raving, Paul; your many books are turning you to madness."
But Paul said: "I am not raving, most excellent Festus; rather, I am speaking words of truth and purity.
For the king knows about this, and to him I speak boldly, for I do not believe that it is hidden from him, nor was this done in a hidden place.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe."
And Agrippa said to Paul: "A little more, and you will persuade me to become a Christian."
And Paul said to him: "I pray to God, whether with little or with much, that not only you but all who hear me may become as I am, except for these bonds."
Then the king rose, and the governors, and Bernice, and those who were sitting with them.
And when they had gone aside, they spoke to one another and said: "This man is doing nothing deserving death or bonds."
And Agrippa said to Festus: "This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar."
And when it was decided that we should sail to Rome, they handed over Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort.
We boarded a ship of Adramyttium that was going to the places of Asia, and set sail. With us was Aristarchus the Macedonian.
And the next day we reached Sidon. Julius showed kindness to Paul and allowed him to go to his friends, so that he might receive provisions.
And from there we went on board and sailed past Cyprus, because the wind was against us.
Then we crossed the deep sea of Cilicia and came to the city of Myra, which is in Lycia.
And there the centurion found a ship of Alexandria that was going to Italy, and he put us on board it.
We sailed slowly for many days and reached Cnidus with difficulty, because the wind would not let us go on. And we sailed past Crete off Salmone.
And when we had passed it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
And as much time had passed and sailing was now dangerous for the ship, because the Fast was already over, Paul spoke to them
and said to them: "Men, I see that there will be hardship and loss, not only of the cargo and of the ship, but our own lives too will be lost along with the ship."
But the centurion trusted the ship's pilot and the ship's owner more than Paul's words.

And since it was not a suitable place to spend the winter, many of them [?] decided to set out from there, in case they could somehow reach Phoenix and spend the winter there, at that harbor of Crete which faced north and toward the land [?].
And a wind blew from the south, and they thought that things would go as they wished. They set out from Asson and sailed along by Crete.
Not much time had passed before a whirlwind struck it, one that is called the "Broad Surge."
And when it seized the ship and the ship could not be turned to face the wind, we gave way and were driven this way and that.
We came under the shelter of a small island called Cauda, and with difficulty we managed to secure the ship's boat,
which they hoisted up. They used supports and bound them around the ship. And fearing that they might run aground on the steep banks, they let down the ship's gear, and so it was driven along.
And as we were in a great storm, the next day they began throwing the cargo overboard.
And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands.
Neither star nor sun appeared for many days, because the storm was great. From then on we gave up all hope of being saved.

And they had gone without food for a long time. Then Paul stood up among them and said: "Men, you should have listened to me and not set out from Crete, and then you would not have brought on yourselves this hardship and loss.
And now I tell you too: take courage, for not one of you will lose his life, only the ship will be lost.
For this night an angel of God stood beside me, the God to whom I belong and whom I serve,
and said to me: 'Do not be afraid, Paul! You must stand before Caesar, and see, God has granted you all who are with you in this ship.'
So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will be just as he told me.
We will be cast ashore on some island."
When the fourteenth night came and we were being driven about in the Adriatic Sea, around midnight the sailors thought they were nearing some land.
And they let down the sounding line and it was twenty fathoms; and after waiting a little they measured again, and it was twelve fathoms.
And fearing that they might run onto a rocky place, they let down four anchors from the stern of the ship and prayed for day to break.
But the sailors meant to flee from the ship, and they let the boat down into the sea, on the pretext of putting out the anchors.
Then Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers: "If these men do not stay in this ship, you cannot be saved."
Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it go, and the waves carried it away.
And as day was breaking, Paul urged everyone to take food, and said: "Today is the fourteenth day since we came, and you have stayed without eating and have taken nothing.
So I urge you to take food, for this is for your survival; for not one hair of the head of any of you will be lost."
And when he had said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.
They all took heart, and they too asked for food.
All of us in the ship numbered two hundred and seventy-six people.
And when they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship, throwing the wheat out of the ship into the sea.
And when day broke, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a shore, onto which they intended to drive the ship if they somehow could.
And they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, and at the same time they loosened the lashings of the rudders, raised the small sail, and held toward the shore with the wind.
And when they ran into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground, and the bow stuck fast and stood immovable, but the stern was being broken up by the violence of the waves.
And the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim away and escape.
But the centurion wanted to save Paul, and he held them back from their plan. He ordered those who could swim to get out by swimming,
and the rest to get out, some on planks and some on other pieces of the ship. And so we came out, and all of us got safely to land.
And once we had come ashore, they learned that the island was called Malta.
And the heathen people there showed us no small kindness, for they lit a fire and took us all in, because of the rain that was falling and the cold.
And as Paul was gathering a large bundle of brushwood and putting it on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.
When the heathen people saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to one another: "This man must be a murderer. Though he escaped the sea, justice has not let him live."
But he shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no harm.

They expected that he would swell up and suddenly fall down dead. But after they had stood and watched for a long time and nothing bad happened to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
In that area there were estates belonging to a certain chief man of the island, whose name was Publius. He took us in and lodged us kindly and with love.
And the father of Publius was lying sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
And when this had happened, others on the island who had illnesses also came and were healed.
They honoured us with many honours, and when we departed they supplied us with provisions.
And after three days we boarded a ship of Alexandria that had wintered at the island, named the Dioscuri.
And we went down to Syracuse and stayed there three days.
From there we sailed around and reached Rhegium. And after one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
where we found brothers, and they begged us to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
From there the brothers heard about us and came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
And when he entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

And after three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. And when they had gathered, he said to them: "Men, brothers, I have done nothing evil against the people or the law of our fathers, yet I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
They examined me and wanted to release me, because I was guilty of nothing that deserved death.
But when the Jews spoke against me, I was forced to appeal to Caesar. It was not that I had any accusation to bring against my own nation.
For this reason I asked you to come, so that I might see you and speak with you, because I wear this chain for the sake of the hope of Israel."
And they said to him: "We have received no letters about you from Judea, and none of the brothers has come and reported or said anything evil about you.
But we ask you to let us hear from you what you think. For we know that everywhere people speak against this sect."

And they set a day, and many came to him at his lodging. From morning until evening he taught them and testified to the kingdom of God, and tried to persuade them about Jesus from the law of Moses and from the prophets.
And some believed his words, and some did not believe.
They were agreed [?] with one another and began to leave. Paul said one thing: "The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
when he said: 'Go to this people and say to them: You will keep on hearing but will not understand, and you will keep on looking but will not see.

For the heart of this people has grown dull, and their ears are hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, so that they may not see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.'
So let it be known to you that this salvation has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen."
And when he had said this, the Jews left, arguing hard among themselves.
And he stayed there two whole years at his own expense, and he welcomed all who came to him.
He preached the kingdom of God and taught about Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without hindrance.
